Summary of 我折腾过的群晖总结 (https://meta.appinn.net/t/topic/7930), 18 posts:

## Original post

Qingwa (#1) explains why discussions rarely mention "black" (unofficial, non-Synology hardware running DSM): official Synology units have pushed them out, and they have been idle for a long time. He lists the trade-offs:

- **Black units (黑群)** offer better hardware for the same money and run the same system. Drawbacks: DSM must be hacked to install, they can't upgrade to the latest system quickly, and their power draw ranges from tens to hundreds of watts.
- **White units (白群, official Synology)** are stable, power-efficient (he says the DS218+ reads under 18 W), and secure. They need no hacking, receive updates immediately, and Synology can offer remote help when something fails.

His recommendation: tinkerers can start with black units, and users with budget to spare should buy official ones. He jokes that black-unit users owe Synology a white unit. He also links about 15 of his own tutorials (DS218+ setup, HTTPS, Plex, Surveillance Station, Docker, ZeroTier, and more). In a 2020 update, he reports that the official 6 GB memory limit can be exceeded: 2×8 GB (16 GB) works plug-and-play.

## What people are saying

- **Alternatives:** allor (#2) asks for an open-source replacement for Synology. Qingwa (#4) suggests FreeNAS (now TrueNAS).
- **Choosing official hardware for convenience:** 9kk (#3) says he bought a Synology years ago because he didn't want to tinker.
- **Negative experience with another brand:** bhqt (#6) reports that a company QNAP unit's network port failed after a few months, and the motherboard had to be replaced. This soured him on Synology too, though the post is ambiguous about which device failed. Others (#7–#11) discuss QNAP's features (such as IFTTT support) and trying it through an online demo or a store.
- **Camera compatibility:** 9kk (#14) asks whether Xiaomi cameras work in Surveillance Station. Qingwa (#15) says it requires a hack and links a community project (yi-hack-v3). 9kk (#16) confirms it's worth trying.
- **Light replies:** Several posts (#5, #12, #13, #17) are jokes or chatter, and one reply (#10) is a playful aside.
- **Lesson learned:** Qingwa (#18) says a reinstall went wrong, but it led him to back up his system for the first time.

Note: the thread mixes posts from 2018 to 2022 and the replies are not in strict date order, so some context may be outdated (for example, DSM versions and hardware specs).

## Tips from the thread

- **Choose by priority:** If you want low cost and are comfortable tinkering, a black unit can be a good choice. If you want stability, low power use, timely updates, and vendor support, buy an official unit.
- **Power and stability are the main arguments for official units:** Consider these factors for a 24/7 home server.
- **Upgrade memory with care:** Qingwa reports that 16 GB works on units officially limited to 6 GB, but that's one user's experience, so check compatibility before buying.
- **Expect some hacking for third-party cameras:** Xiaomi cameras need community firmware or hacks to work in Surveillance Station. Weigh the risks before trying.
- **Back up your system:** The reinstall episode (#18) is a reminder to back up system configuration regularly.
- **Consider alternatives:** TrueNAS (FreeNAS) is an open-source option for NAS builds.
- **Unresolved:** Whether black units remain practical as DSM evolves, and how reliable QNAP and Synology compare, are left to individual experience. The anecdotes in the thread (#6) are not conclusive.

Summary of 离了个大谱：群晖，只有自家硬盘才能兼容并提供全方位的功能和支持 (https://meta.appinn.net/t/topic/70196), 10 posts:

## Original post

Qingwa shared a Synology press release from its German site (DACH region) and linked to an Appinn article about it. The author said they first thought it was a joke. The main points of the announcement:

- **Drive restriction for new Plus models:** Starting with Plus models released in 2025, only Synology drives and third-party drives certified to Synology's specifications will get full functionality and support.
- **Existing models are unaffected:** Plus models released up to 2024 (excluding the XS Plus and rackmount lines) will not change. Moving drives from an existing Synology NAS to a new Plus model remains allowed without restriction.
- **Limits on other drives:** Compatible but unlisted drives will face some restrictions, such as pool creation and support for problems caused by those drives.
- **Features limited to Synology drives:** Volume-level deduplication, lifespan analysis, and automatic drive firmware updates will only work with Synology drives.

The author's tone is sarcastic, summed up as "离了个大谱" (roughly, "this is outrageous").

## What people are saying

- **Firmware limit seems reasonable, lifespan limit does not:** One user found the restriction on automatic firmware updates understandable, but questioned limiting lifespan analysis, arguing that SMART reporting is a basic NAS function #2.
- **Workaround discussed:** Several users noted that drives can be initialized on a non-genuine (black) Synology or an older Synology model and then installed in a new Plus model #3 #5. This suggests the restriction may be easy to get around, though the thread does not confirm whether it works long-term.
- **Skepticism about Synology's dominance:** One user questioned whether Synology is really so dominant that it can make such a move #4.
- **Wording correction:** One user pointed out that the press release says "compatible but unlisted" drives, not "incompatible," and asked which third-party drives are actually certified #6.
- **Market impact jokes and opinions:**
  - One user suggested this favors used Synology sellers #7, but the original poster replied that it benefits domestic (Chinese) vendors #8.
  - A QNAP user expressed amusement, since the move hurts a competitor's customers #9.
  - Another user said it benefits DIY builders and open-source NAS management tools #10.

## Tips from the thread

- **Check before buying:** If you plan to buy a new Plus model, verify which third-party drives are on Synology's certified list. The thread did not identify the list.
- **Existing hardware is safe for now:** Pre-2025 Plus models and drive migration between existing units are not affected, according to the announcement.
- **Expect limits on non-Synology drives:** Even if a non-listed drive works, you may lose pool creation or support, and some features (deduplication, lifespan analysis, automatic firmware updates) may be unavailable.
- **The workaround is unverified:** Initializing drives on another Synology unit and then moving them to a new model was suggested #3 #5, but its reliability and any future restrictions on it remain unknown.
- **Open questions:**
  - Which third-party drives are certified?
  - Does the lifespan analysis restriction really apply, as the press release states?
  - Will Synology close the workaround?
  - How will this affect users in regions beyond DACH?

Summary of 群晖认怂！用户狂喷半年后，最新 DSM 7.3 终于低头：取消专用硬盘限制 (https://meta.appinn.net/t/topic/75519), 20 posts:

## Original post

- **核心消息**：据多家媒体报道，群晖（Synology）将在 DSM 7.3 中取消 HDD 机械硬盘的专用限制，未来 NAS 恢复使用任意硬盘。主要影响 2025 年发布的 Plus 机型，如 DS925+、DS1525+、DS725+、DS1825+、DS425+、DS225+ 和 RS2825RP+。SSD 存储池仍需使用专用或认证 SSD。DSM 7.3 的发布时间尚未确定，可能在 2025 年四季度或 2026 年一季度初。#1
- **事件背景**：2025 年 4 月，群晖宣布新 Plus 机型只支持自有品牌或认证硬盘。4 月 23 日 DS925+ 发布，成为第一款限制第三方硬盘的机型。作者认为这一政策很离谱，并表示自己已转用飞牛 OS。#1
- **作者观点**：群晖近年对家庭用户重视不足，例如砍掉 Video Station，Synology Photos 也落后于飞牛相册和 Immich 等产品。作者认为，对个人和家庭用户来说，DSM 7.3 不足以扭转局面，市场上第三方品牌已经很多，性价比更高；但群晖在文件管理、数据同步、安全和稳定性方面仍很专业，企业用户可能仍会选择它。#1
- **数据来源说明**：群晖销量下滑的说法来自 nascompares 等媒体对欧美渠道的调查，属于转述，原文未给出可核实的具体数字。#1

## What people are saying

- **对群晖的态度**：有人认为群晖"桀骜不驯"的个性有可取之处。#2 也有人担心飞牛的发展路线像 MIUI 初期，未来可能露出不同面貌，因此计划下次配置 OMV。#3
- **飞牛的定位**：作者和其他用户都认为飞牛做影视 NAS 不错，但其他功能暂时还不成熟。#5
- **对厂商的批评**：有用户指出台湾厂商容易走 HTC 的老路，DS9 系列甚至开始取消硬件解码支持。#6
- **用户迁移的实际做法**：
  - starmoon 因硬盘限制和媒体功能被削弱，换成了 1522+。后来考虑绿联 6800 Pro，但因价格虚高没有入手，最终购入一台 48p 16G 作媒体播放，并保留白群 15 做数据存储。#7 #19
  - 有用户提醒，群晖在一些非 Plus 或特定版本中仍有驱动和兼容性问题：不在列表中的 M2 盘无法创建缓存盘；7.2.2 某版本砍掉了第三方万兆网卡识别，只能手动加载驱动。该用户已关闭自动更新，担心 7.3 再砍驱动。#9
- **企业市场**：有人认为企业不太可能选群晖，HPE、Dell、H3C 等更可靠。#8 也有人认为连锁机构可能在分支机构采购群晖作为本地存储，主要用于本地读写。#10 另有用户指出，企业即便有不同政策，也不敢买，因为被厂商绑定的商业服务会带来安全风险。#20
- **换系统的经验与教训**：一位用户从 OMV 迁移到飞牛后遇到多个问题：旧系统创建的软 RAID 无法识别，只能以链接方式使用；系统应用权限异常；80、443、5432 等端口被飞牛占用；访问项目时经常长时间卡顿；在 120G SSD 上运行三万多小时、写入达 71T 后损坏。#13 作者和其他用户都建议直接从零安装飞牛，而不是在旧系统上迁移。#14 #15
- **整机推荐**：有用户想买整机 NAS 存重要数据，作者不太敢推荐第三方，认为省心还是群晖，可以考虑二手 DS24 系列。#16 #17
- **硬盘价格**：有用户指出硬盘价格大涨，新用户的购买门槛上升，因此暂时不急于购买。#18
- **讨论风格**：有用户怀疑原文是 AI 润色的，作者回应只有配图是 AI 生成，正文是带着情绪写的。#11 #12

## Tips from the thread

- **购买前先确认具体机型和硬盘类型**：DSM 7.3 目前只确认取消 HDD 限制，SSD 存储池和缓存仍需专用盘。M2 盘也要看兼容列表。#1 #9
- **不要急于等待 DSM 7.3**：发布时间未定，且取消限制的范围和兼容性仍需观察。#1
- **升级前关闭自动更新**：大版本可能砍掉驱动或功能，如网卡、硬件解码等，建议先看更新说明。#6 #9
- **换系统尽量全新安装**：从旧系统迁移容易出现 RAID 识别、端口冲突和权限问题，建议清空后重装。#13 #14 #15
- **注意系统盘寿命**：系统盘频繁写入可能导致 SSD 提前损坏，尤其是小容量消费级盘，应定期检查写入量。#13

## Original post

Qingwa shared a article (neil.computer, "how to set up a minimal ZFS NAS without TrueNAS") and summarized its main arguments in Chinese:

- **Core need:** manage disks with ZFS, share files on the LAN, keep data reliable and easy to recover.
- **Use plain Debian instead of a NAS OS:** Debian + OpenZFS + Samba is enough. TrueNAS, Synology-style systems and Feiniu bring web UIs, app stores, VMs and Docker that a pure storage box doesn't need.
- **ZFS is the core:** software RAIDZ, checksums, self-healing with redundancy, snapshots, compression, and per-dataset configuration.
- **Configuration lives on the disks:** if the OS disk dies, reinstalling Debian and OpenZFS brings back the pool, datasets and snapshots without rebuilding the RAID.
- **Low maintenance:** mainly periodic `zpool scrub` and occasional `zpool status` checks.
- **Separate storage from compute:** run Jellyfin, Immich, Home Assistant etc. on another machine and access the NAS over SMB/NFS. Qingwa also flagged this as impractical for people with only one machine.
- **Docker:** the author didn't need it, but it can coexist with ZFS on Debian.
- **Conclusion:** don't install a NAS OS just for a NAS; a hand-built system works well and has no management UI.

## What people are saying

**Storage vs. compute split**
- Several agree it's ideal in principle, but most people run everything on one box. Niceb notes that a Mac mini running Docker keeps filling its local disk, though it can be fixed #6.
- Qingwa acknowledged the one-machine case is common #1.
- syun argues storage-compute separation is best, and even an ARM box is enough for storage, while a basic x86 quad-core suffices for home compute #14.

**RAID and data loss**
- t35t asked what happens if a data disk fails. Niceb answered that RAID1/RAID5 helps to a degree, but multi-location backups (NAS, cloud) are the real safeguard #3 #5.
- Qingwa clarified that the article means you don't need to *recreate* RAID after reinstalling the OS, not that RAID is unnecessary #4 #7.
- syun takes a contrarian view: at home, RAID isn't worth it. It was designed for service continuity, not backup. RAID can degrade during power events, and tiered storage can lose data if a sudden outage hits mid-sync. Cross-machine sync is more useful #14. syun later suggested one NAS as a sync hub, with hot data on both the PC and NAS, sensitive photos encrypted in cloud storage, and never keeping all copies in one place #17.

**Hardware and reliability**
- WhiteHorse says current disk prices have pushed them away from NAS #13. t35t also said rising storage prices made them shelve a plan to buy a NAS for family photos and videos #3.
- gigacore argues most consumer NAS builds use unreliable hardware, and reports that memtest86 found bit flips on their own machine about once every two days #15. gigacore recommends a stable, older platform (e.g., DDR4 Zen 3 in 2026) and keeping the storage machine free of extra workloads #12.
- SmallPackage reports a small home server running for over a year without issues, while overclocked desktop RAM caused constant crashes #16.

**Software choice**
- VictoryRoad suggests FreeBSD for the best ZFS support #9. xmmdg recalled using FreeNAS (which is FreeBSD-based, not OpenBSD) as their first ZFS exposure #10 #11. gigacore notes OpenBSD performs poorly, e.g., disabling hyperthreading by default, and FreeBSD is the production-grade BSD #12.

**Usability and the NAS market**
- SmallPackage observes that most people really want a home server, and NAS products are simply the closest mature option #8.
- gigacore says NAS systems are hard to use, even for professionals who still look things up, and that vendors overemphasize app capabilities #12.
- gigacore also warns that exposing NAS ports directly to the internet is risky and that few people actually follow 3-2-1 backups #12.

- **Backups matter more than RAID.** RAID protects against disk failure and downtime, not accidental deletion, ransomware or a single-site disaster. Keep at least one copy off the NAS (another machine, external disk or cloud). Encrypt sensitive cloud copies.

Summary of 我折腾过的群晖总结 (https://meta.appinn.net/t/topic/7930), 18 posts:

## Original post

Qingwa (#1) explains why discussions rarely mention "black" (unofficial, non-Synology hardware running DSM): official Synology units have pushed them out, and they have been idle for a long time. He lists the trade-offs:

- **Black units (黑群)** offer better hardware for the same money and run the same system. Drawbacks: DSM must be hacked to install, they can't upgrade to the latest system quickly, and their power draw ranges from tens to hundreds of watts.
- **White units (白群, official Synology)** are stable, power-efficient (he says the DS218+ reads under 18 W), and secure. They need no hacking, receive updates immediately, and Synology can offer remote help when something fails.

His recommendation: tinkerers can start with black units, and users with budget to spare should buy official ones. He jokes that black-unit users owe Synology a white unit. He also links about 15 of his own tutorials (DS218+ setup, HTTPS, Plex, Surveillance Station, Docker, ZeroTier, and more). In a 2020 update, he reports that the official 6 GB memory limit can be exceeded: 2×8 GB (16 GB) works plug-and-play.

## What people are saying

- **Alternatives:** allor (#2) asks for an open-source replacement for Synology. Qingwa (#4) suggests FreeNAS (now TrueNAS).
- **Choosing official hardware for convenience:** 9kk (#3) says he bought a Synology years ago because he didn't want to tinker.
- **Negative experience with another brand:** bhqt (#6) reports that a company QNAP unit's network port failed after a few months, and the motherboard had to be replaced. This soured him on Synology too, though the post is ambiguous about which device failed. Others (#7–#11) discuss QNAP's features (such as IFTTT support) and trying it through an online demo or a store.
- **Camera compatibility:** 9kk (#14) asks whether Xiaomi cameras work in Surveillance Station. Qingwa (#15) says it requires a hack and links a community project (yi-hack-v3). 9kk (#16) confirms it's worth trying.
- **Light replies:** Several posts (#5, #12, #13, #17) are jokes or chatter, and one reply (#10) is a playful aside.
- **Lesson learned:** Qingwa (#18) says a reinstall went wrong, but it led him to back up his system for the first time.

Note: the thread mixes posts from 2018 to 2022 and the replies are not in strict date order, so some context may be outdated (for example, DSM versions and hardware specs).

## Tips from the thread

- **Choose by priority:** If you want low cost and are comfortable tinkering, a black unit can be a good choice. If you want stability, low power use, timely updates, and vendor support, buy an official unit.
- **Power and stability are the main arguments for official units:** Consider these factors for a 24/7 home server.
- **Upgrade memory with care:** Qingwa reports that 16 GB works on units officially limited to 6 GB, but that's one user's experience, so check compatibility before buying.
- **Expect some hacking for third-party cameras:** Xiaomi cameras need community firmware or hacks to work in Surveillance Station. Weigh the risks before trying.
- **Back up your system:** The reinstall episode (#18) is a reminder to back up system configuration regularly.
- **Consider alternatives:** TrueNAS (FreeNAS) is an open-source option for NAS builds.
- **Unresolved:** Whether black units remain practical as DSM evolves, and how reliable QNAP and Synology compare, are left to individual experience. The anecdotes in the thread (#6) are not conclusive.

## Original post

Qingwa shared a Synology press release from its German site (DACH region) and linked to an Appinn article about it. The author said they first thought it was a joke. The main points of the announcement:

- **Drive restriction for new Plus models:** Starting with Plus models released in 2025, only Synology drives and third-party drives certified to Synology's specifications will get full functionality and support.
- **Existing models are unaffected:** Plus models released up to 2024 (excluding the XS Plus and rackmount lines) will not change. Moving drives from an existing Synology NAS to a new Plus model remains allowed without restriction.
- **Limits on other drives:** Compatible but unlisted drives will face some restrictions, such as pool creation and support for problems caused by those drives.
- **Features limited to Synology drives:** Volume-level deduplication, lifespan analysis, and automatic drive firmware updates will only work with Synology drives.

The author's tone is sarcastic, summed up as "离了个大谱" (roughly, "this is outrageous").

## What people are saying

- **Firmware limit seems reasonable, lifespan limit does not:** One user found the restriction on automatic firmware updates understandable, but questioned limiting lifespan analysis, arguing that SMART reporting is a basic NAS function #2.
- **Workaround discussed:** Several users noted that drives can be initialized on a non-genuine (black) Synology or an older Synology model and then installed in a new Plus model #3 #5. This suggests the restriction may be easy to get around, though the thread does not confirm whether it works long-term.
- **Skepticism about Synology's dominance:** One user questioned whether Synology is really so dominant that it can make such a move #4.
- **Wording correction:** One user pointed out that the press release says "compatible but unlisted" drives, not "incompatible," and asked which third-party drives are actually certified #6.
- **Market impact jokes and opinions:**
  - One user suggested this favors used Synology sellers #7, but the original poster replied that it benefits domestic (Chinese) vendors #8.
  - A QNAP user expressed amusement, since the move hurts a competitor's customers #9.
  - Another user said it benefits DIY builders and open-source NAS management tools #10.

## Tips from the thread

- **Check before buying:** If you plan to buy a new Plus model, verify which third-party drives are on Synology's certified list. The thread did not identify the list.
- **Existing hardware is safe for now:** Pre-2025 Plus models and drive migration between existing units are not affected, according to the announcement.
- **Expect limits on non-Synology drives:** Even if a non-listed drive works, you may lose pool creation or support, and some features (deduplication, lifespan analysis, automatic firmware updates) may be unavailable.
- **The workaround is unverified:** Initializing drives on another Synology unit and then moving them to a new model was suggested #3 #5, but its reliability and any future restrictions on it remain unknown.
- **Open questions:**
  - Which third-party drives are certified?
  - Does the lifespan analysis restriction really apply, as the press release states?
  - Will Synology close the workaround?
  - How will this affect users in regions beyond DACH?

Summary of 最纯粹的 NAS：直接上 ZFS (https://meta.appinn.net/t/topic/87972), 18 posts:

## Original post

Qingwa shared a article (neil.computer, "how to set up a minimal ZFS NAS without TrueNAS") and summarized its main arguments in Chinese:

- **Core need:** manage disks with ZFS, share files on the LAN, keep data reliable and easy to recover.
- **Use plain Debian instead of a NAS OS:** Debian + OpenZFS + Samba is enough. TrueNAS, Synology-style systems and Feiniu bring web UIs, app stores, VMs and Docker that a pure storage box doesn't need.
- **ZFS is the core:** software RAIDZ, checksums, self-healing with redundancy, snapshots, compression, and per-dataset configuration.
- **Configuration lives on the disks:** if the OS disk dies, reinstalling Debian and OpenZFS brings back the pool, datasets and snapshots without rebuilding the RAID.
- **Low maintenance:** mainly periodic `zpool scrub` and occasional `zpool status` checks.
- **Separate storage from compute:** run Jellyfin, Immich, Home Assistant etc. on another machine and access the NAS over SMB/NFS. Qingwa also flagged this as impractical for people with only one machine.
- **Docker:** the author didn't need it, but it can coexist with ZFS on Debian.
- **Conclusion:** don't install a NAS OS just for a NAS; a hand-built system works well and has no management UI.

## What people are saying

**Storage vs. compute split**
- Several agree it's ideal in principle, but most people run everything on one box. Niceb notes that a Mac mini running Docker keeps filling its local disk, though it can be fixed #6.
- Qingwa acknowledged the one-machine case is common #1.
- syun argues storage-compute separation is best, and even an ARM box is enough for storage, while a basic x86 quad-core suffices for home compute #14.

**RAID and data loss**
- t35t asked what happens if a data disk fails. Niceb answered that RAID1/RAID5 helps to a degree, but multi-location backups (NAS, cloud) are the real safeguard #3 #5.
- Qingwa clarified that the article means you don't need to *recreate* RAID after reinstalling the OS, not that RAID is unnecessary #4 #7.
- syun takes a contrarian view: at home, RAID isn't worth it. It was designed for service continuity, not backup. RAID can degrade during power events, and tiered storage can lose data if a sudden outage hits mid-sync. Cross-machine sync is more useful #14. syun later suggested one NAS as a sync hub, with hot data on both the PC and NAS, sensitive photos encrypted in cloud storage, and never keeping all copies in one place #17.

**Hardware and reliability**
- WhiteHorse says current disk prices have pushed them away from NAS #13. t35t also said rising storage prices made them shelve a plan to buy a NAS for family photos and videos #3.
- gigacore argues most consumer NAS builds use unreliable hardware, and reports that memtest86 found bit flips on their own machine about once every two days #15. gigacore recommends a stable, older platform (e.g., DDR4 Zen 3 in 2026) and keeping the storage machine free of extra workloads #12.
- SmallPackage reports a small home server running for over a year without issues, while overclocked desktop RAM caused constant crashes #16.

**Software choice**
- VictoryRoad suggests FreeBSD for the best ZFS support #9. xmmdg recalled using FreeNAS (which is FreeBSD-based, not OpenBSD) as their first ZFS exposure #10 #11. gigacore notes OpenBSD performs poorly, e.g., disabling hyperthreading by default, and FreeBSD is the production-grade BSD #12.

**Usability and the NAS market**
- SmallPackage observes that most people really want a home server, and NAS products are simply the closest mature option #8.
- gigacore says NAS systems are hard to use, even for professionals who still look things up, and that vendors overemphasize app capabilities #12.
- gigacore also warns that exposing NAS ports directly to the internet is risky and that few people actually follow 3-2-1 backups #12.
- allor's one-line stack for a home box: Debian + Samba + various Docker containers + a simple landing page #18.

**Notable contributors:** syun (most detailed on RAID and backup strategy #14 #17), gigacore (hardware and security perspective #12 #15), Niceb (practical backup advice #5).

## Tips from the thread

- **Backups matter more than RAID.** RAID protects against disk failure and downtime, not accidental deletion, ransomware or a single-site disaster. Keep at least one copy off the NAS (another machine, external disk or cloud). Encrypt sensitive cloud copies.
- **Don't misread "no need to recreate RAID."** The article means ZFS metadata is stored on the pool disks, so the array survives an OS reinstall. You still need redundancy for disk failures.
- **Run regular scrubs and check `zpool status`.** This is the low-effort maintenance routine the article recommends #1.
- **Use stable hardware for storage.** Test RAM (e.g., memtest86) before trusting a box with data, and avoid overclocking on a storage machine #12 #15 #16.
- **Keep the storage box lean.** Disabling unused services (as one user did with Synology #2) and avoiding heavy workloads on the storage host reduces risk #12.
- **Consider a split setup if practical.** A small, always-on storage machine plus separate compute is the cleanest design, but a single well-configured box is acceptable for many households #6 #14.
- **Be cautious about internet exposure.** Don't open NAS ports directly to the internet #12.

**Unresolved questions**
- Whether RAID is worth it for home use (opinions diverge: syun against, others for RAID1/RAID5 #5).
- Best approach to backups on a tight budget with rising storage prices #3 #13.
- Which OS is best for ZFS at home: Debian with OpenZFS (the article's choice) versus FreeBSD/TrueNAS, which was only touched on briefly #9 #10.

Summary of 我折腾过的群晖总结 (https://meta.appinn.net/t/topic/7930), 18 posts:

## Original post

Qingwa (#1) explains why discussions rarely mention "black" (unofficial, non-Synology hardware running DSM): official Synology units have pushed them out, and they have been idle for a long time. He lists the trade-offs:

- **Black units (黑群)** offer better hardware for the same money and run the same system. Drawbacks: DSM must be hacked to install, they can't upgrade to the latest system quickly, and their power draw ranges from tens to hundreds of watts.
- **White units (白群, official Synology)** are stable, power-efficient (he says the DS218+ reads under 18 W), and secure. They need no hacking, receive updates immediately, and Synology can offer remote help when something fails.

His recommendation: tinkerers can start with black units, and users with budget to spare should buy official ones. He jokes that black-unit users owe Synology a white unit. He also links about 15 of his own tutorials (DS218+ setup, HTTPS, Plex, Surveillance Station, Docker, ZeroTier, and more). In a 2020 update, he reports that the official 6 GB memory limit can be exceeded: 2×8 GB (16 GB) works plug-and-play.

## What people are saying

- **Alternatives:** allor (#2) asks for an open-source replacement for Synology. Qingwa (#4) suggests FreeNAS (now TrueNAS).
- **Choosing official hardware for convenience:** 9kk (#3) says he bought a Synology years ago because he didn't want to tinker.
- **Negative experience with another brand:** bhqt (#6) reports that a company QNAP unit's network port failed after a few months, and the motherboard had to be replaced. This soured him on Synology too, though the post is ambiguous about which device failed. Others (#7–#11) discuss QNAP's features (such as IFTTT support) and trying it through an online demo or a store.
- **Camera compatibility:** 9kk (#14) asks whether Xiaomi cameras work in Surveillance Station. Qingwa (#15) says it requires a hack and links a community project (yi-hack-v3). 9kk (#16) confirms it's worth trying.
- **Light replies:** Several posts (#5, #12, #13, #17) are jokes or chatter, and one reply (#10) is a playful aside.
- **Lesson learned:** Qingwa (#18) says a reinstall went wrong, but it led him to back up his system for the first time.

Note: the thread mixes posts from 2018 to 2022 and the replies are not in strict date order, so some context may be outdated (for example, DSM versions and hardware specs).

## Tips from the thread

- **Choose by priority:** If you want low cost and are comfortable tinkering, a black unit can be a good choice. If you want stability, low power use, timely updates, and vendor support, buy an official unit.
- **Power and stability are the main arguments for official units:** Consider these factors for a 24/7 home server.
- **Upgrade memory with care:** Qingwa reports that 16 GB works on units officially limited to 6 GB, but that's one user's experience, so check compatibility before buying.
- **Expect some hacking for third-party cameras:** Xiaomi cameras need community firmware or hacks to work in Surveillance Station. Weigh the risks before trying.
- **Back up your system:** The reinstall episode (#18) is a reminder to back up system configuration regularly.
- **Consider alternatives:** TrueNAS (FreeNAS) is an open-source option for NAS builds.
- **Unresolved:** Whether black units remain practical as DSM evolves, and how reliable QNAP and Synology compare, are left to individual experience. The anecdotes in the thread (#6) are not conclusive.

## Original post

Qingwa shared a Synology press release from its German site (DACH region) and linked to an Appinn article about it. The author said they first thought it was a joke. The main points of the announcement:

- **Drive restriction for new Plus models:** Starting with Plus models released in 2025, only Synology drives and third-party drives certified to Synology's specifications will get full functionality and support.
- **Existing models are unaffected:** Plus models released up to 2024 (excluding the XS Plus and rackmount lines) will not change. Moving drives from an existing Synology NAS to a new Plus model remains allowed without restriction.
- **Limits on other drives:** Compatible but unlisted drives will face some restrictions, such as pool creation and support for problems caused by those drives.
- **Features limited to Synology drives:** Volume-level deduplication, lifespan analysis, and automatic drive firmware updates will only work with Synology drives.

The author's tone is sarcastic, summed up as "离了个大谱" (roughly, "this is outrageous").

## What people are saying

- **Firmware limit seems reasonable, lifespan limit does not:** One user found the restriction on automatic firmware updates understandable, but questioned limiting lifespan analysis, arguing that SMART reporting is a basic NAS function #2.
- **Workaround discussed:** Several users noted that drives can be initialized on a non-genuine (black) Synology or an older Synology model and then installed in a new Plus model #3 #5. This suggests the restriction may be easy to get around, though the thread does not confirm whether it works long-term.
- **Skepticism about Synology's dominance:** One user questioned whether Synology is really so dominant that it can make such a move #4.
- **Wording correction:** One user pointed out that the press release says "compatible but unlisted" drives, not "incompatible," and asked which third-party drives are actually certified #6.
- **Market impact jokes and opinions:**
  - One user suggested this favors used Synology sellers #7, but the original poster replied that it benefits domestic (Chinese) vendors #8.
  - A QNAP user expressed amusement, since the move hurts a competitor's customers #9.
  - Another user said it benefits DIY builders and open-source NAS management tools #10.

## Tips from the thread

- **Check before buying:** If you plan to buy a new Plus model, verify which third-party drives are on Synology's certified list. The thread did not identify the list.
- **Existing hardware is safe for now:** Pre-2025 Plus models and drive migration between existing units are not affected, according to the announcement.
- **Expect limits on non-Synology drives:** Even if a non-listed drive works, you may lose pool creation or support, and some features (deduplication, lifespan analysis, automatic firmware updates) may be unavailable.
- **The workaround is unverified:** Initializing drives on another Synology unit and then moving them to a new model was suggested #3 #5, but its reliability and any future restrictions on it remain unknown.
- **Open questions:**
  - Which third-party drives are certified?
  - Does the lifespan analysis restriction really apply, as the press release states?
  - Will Synology close the workaround?
  - How will this affect users in regions beyond DACH?

Qingwa shared a article (neil.computer, "how to set up a minimal ZFS NAS without TrueNAS") and summarized its main arguments in Chinese:

- **Core need:** manage disks with ZFS, share files on the LAN, keep data reliable and easy to recover.
- **Use plain Debian instead of a NAS OS:** Debian + OpenZFS + Samba is enough. TrueNAS, Synology-style systems and Feiniu bring web UIs, app stores, VMs and Docker that a pure storage box doesn't need.
- **ZFS is the core:** software RAIDZ, checksums, self-healing with redundancy, snapshots, compression, and per-dataset configuration.
- **Configuration lives on the disks:** if the OS disk dies, reinstalling Debian and OpenZFS brings back the pool, datasets and snapshots without rebuilding the RAID.
- **Low maintenance:** mainly periodic `zpool scrub` and occasional `zpool status` checks.
- **Separate storage from compute:** run Jellyfin, Immich, Home Assistant etc. on another machine and access the NAS over SMB/NFS. Qingwa also flagged this as impractical for people with only one machine.
- **Docker:** the author didn't need it, but it can coexist with ZFS on Debian.
- **Conclusion:** don't install a NAS OS just for a NAS; a hand-built system works well and has no management UI.

## What people are saying

**Storage vs. compute split**
- Several agree it's ideal in principle, but most people run everything on one box. Niceb notes that a Mac mini running Docker keeps filling its local disk, though it can be fixed #6.
- Qingwa acknowledged the one-machine case is common #1.
- syun argues storage-compute separation is best, and even an ARM box is enough for storage, while a basic x86 quad-core suffices for home compute #14.

**RAID and data loss**
- t35t asked what happens if a data disk fails. Niceb answered that RAID1/RAID5 helps to a degree, but multi-location backups (NAS, cloud) are the real safeguard #3 #5.
- Qingwa clarified that the article means you don't need to *recreate* RAID after reinstalling the OS, not that RAID is unnecessary #4 #7.
- syun takes a contrarian view: at home, RAID isn't worth it. It was designed for service continuity, not backup. RAID can degrade during power events, and tiered storage can lose data if a sudden outage hits mid-sync. Cross-machine sync is more useful #14. syun later suggested one NAS as a sync hub, with hot data on both the PC and NAS, sensitive photos encrypted in cloud storage, and never keeping all copies in one place #17.

**Hardware and reliability**
- WhiteHorse says current disk prices have pushed them away from NAS #13. t35t also said rising storage prices made them shelve a plan to buy a NAS for family photos and videos #3.
- gigacore argues most consumer NAS builds use unreliable hardware, and reports that memtest86 found bit flips on their own machine about once every two days #15. gigacore recommends a stable, older platform (e.g., DDR4 Zen 3 in 2026) and keeping the storage machine free of extra workloads #12.
- SmallPackage reports a small home server running for over a year without issues, while overclocked desktop RAM caused constant crashes #16.

**Software choice**
- VictoryRoad suggests FreeBSD for the best ZFS support #9. xmmdg recalled using FreeNAS (which is FreeBSD-based, not OpenBSD) as their first ZFS exposure #10 #11. gigacore notes OpenBSD performs poorly, e.g., disabling hyperthreading by default, and FreeBSD is the production-grade BSD #12.

**Usability and the NAS market**
- SmallPackage observes that most people really want a home server, and NAS products are simply the closest mature option #8.
- gigacore says NAS systems are hard to use, even for professionals who still look things up, and that vendors overemphasize app capabilities #12.

- **Backups matter more than RAID.** RAID protects against disk failure and downtime, not accidental deletion, ransomware or a single-site disaster. Keep at least one copy off the NAS (another machine, external disk or cloud). Encrypt sensitive cloud copies.

- **Be cautious about internet exposure.** Don't open NAS ports directly to the internet #12.

- Whether RAID is worth it for home use (opinions diverge: syun against, others for RAID1/RAID5 #5).
- Best approach to backups on a tight budget with rising storage prices #3 #13.
- Which OS is best for ZFS at home: Debian with OpenZFS (the article's choice) versus FreeBSD/TrueNAS, which was only touched on briefly #9 #10.
